theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one-word term describes assets that have no physical form, such as brands, know-how and customer lists?
Which one-word legal right protects original works such as books, music, photographs and software code?
What two-word term names a sign, such as a name or logo, that distinguishes a firm's goods or services from others'?
What one-word legal right gives an inventor the sole right to use a new invention for a set period?
A design licence earns J$750,000 a year. How much does it earn over a four-year licence term, in J$?
What three-letter short form names an agreement in which a person promises to keep shared information secret?
What one-word term names the value of a firm's reputation and customer loyalty, often recognised when the firm is sold?
What one-word term names the use of someone else's intellectual property without permission?
What one-word term names an arrangement in which one firm lets others trade under its brand and system in return for fees?
What one-word term names a payment made to the owner of intellectual property for each sale or use under a licence?
What one-word term names the spreading of the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life?
What two-word term names the website address a firm registers, such as one ending in ".com"?
What two-word term names valuable business information, such as a recipe or process, that is protected by keeping it confidential rather than registering it?
What one-word term names the person or firm that grants a licence to use its intellectual property?
Royalty income was J$1,800,000 last year and rose by 15% this year. What is this year's royalty income, in J$?

essays.stem: Explain how you would identify the intangible assets of a medium-sized food manufacturer in St Catherine and set up a register to manage them.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by explaining to the managers what intangible assets are and why they matter, then hold short meetings with each department to list them. Marketing would identify brand names, logos, labels, the website, domain names and social media accounts. Production would identify recipes, processes and any special equipment designs. Sales would identify customer and distributor lists, contracts and long-standing relationships. Human resources would identify key staff know-how and training materials. Finance and legal would identify licences, permits, registrations and agreements already in place. I would check which assets are registered, for example trade marks, and which rely on secrecy or contracts. I would then set up a register, in a secure spreadsheet, with columns for each asset's description, type, owner in the firm, how it is protected, registration numbers and countries, renewal dates, its importance to the business, risks and the action needed. The register would be held by a named manager, with access limited to those who need it. Renewal dates would be put into a calendar with reminders. The register would be reviewed every year, and whenever a new product, contract or brand is created.
markingPoints: Involves each department to identify a wide range of intangible assets
Checks how each asset is currently protected
Sets up a register with suitable details, including owners and renewal dates
Keeps the register secure with a named person responsible
Reviews and updates the register regularly

essays.stem: Compare copyright, trade marks, patents and trade secrets as ways to protect intangible assets, and say which suits each of these: a company logo, a training video, a new machine part and a sauce recipe.
essays.modelAnswer: Copyright protects original creative works such as writing, music, photographs, films and software. It usually arises automatically when the work is created, so no registration is needed, but it protects the expression, not the idea behind it. A trade mark protects a name, logo or other sign that identifies a firm's goods or services. It is strongest when registered with the national intellectual property office, can be renewed as long as it is used, and is registered country by country. A patent protects a new, inventive and industrially useful invention, giving the owner the sole right to use it for a limited period. It must be applied for, costs more, and requires the invention to be described publicly, so it must not be disclosed before filing. A trade secret protects valuable confidential information for as long as it is kept secret, with no registration, but protection is lost if the secret leaks or a rival works it out independently. The company logo suits a registered trade mark. The training video is protected by copyright. The new machine part, if truly new, suits a patent. The sauce recipe is usually best kept as a trade secret, protected by limited access and confidentiality agreements.
markingPoints: Explains copyright correctly, including automatic protection
Explains trade marks correctly, including registration by country
Explains patents correctly, including novelty and disclosure
Explains trade secrets correctly, including the risk of leaks
Matches each of the four examples to a suitable form of protection

essays.stem: Describe how a firm can use contracts and good practice with employees, contractors and business partners to protect its intangible assets.
essays.modelAnswer: With employees, the firm should include a confidentiality clause in every employment contract and make clear that work created as part of the job belongs to the firm. Where it is reasonable and allowed by employment law, senior staff may also agree not to approach the firm's customers for a period after they leave. New staff should be told about the firm's intangible assets during induction, and access to sensitive information should be limited to those who need it. When staff leave, the firm should end their access to systems, recover devices and documents, and remind them of their duties. With contractors, such as designers, programmers and consultants, the contract must state that the rights in the work they produce are assigned to the firm, because otherwise the contractor may own them. It should also include confidentiality terms. With business partners, such as manufacturers, distributors and joint venture partners, the firm should sign a non-disclosure agreement before sharing any information, and its contracts should state who owns existing and new intellectual property, how it may be used, quality standards and what happens when the agreement ends. All contracts should be checked by an attorney and stored securely.
markingPoints: Uses confidentiality and ownership terms in employment contracts
Manages staff induction, access and leaving properly
Ensures contractors assign rights in their work to the firm
Uses NDAs and clear IP terms with business partners
Has contracts checked by an attorney and stored securely

essays.stem: A Jamaican snack firm can either license its brand to a manufacturer in Trinidad for a royalty of 6% of sales, expected to be J$50,000,000 a year for three years, or invest J$15,000,000 in its own production there and expect a profit of J$4,500,000 a year. Calculate the three-year return from each option, and recommend which the firm should choose.
essays.modelAnswer: Under the licence, the yearly royalty is 6% of J$50,000,000, which is J$3,000,000, so over three years the firm earns J$9,000,000, with very little investment of its own. Under its own production, profit over three years is 3 times J$4,500,000, which is J$13,500,000. Taking away the investment of J$15,000,000 leaves a net shortfall of J$1,500,000 after three years, before allowing for any value the plant still has. On these figures, licensing gives a better return over three years and much lower risk, because the firm does not have to fund a factory, hire staff or manage operations abroad. However, licensing has risks of its own. The firm depends on the licensee to make good products and to report sales honestly, and poor quality could damage the brand in Jamaica as well as in Trinidad. I would recommend licensing, but only with a strong agreement: the brand must be registered as a trade mark in Trinidad, the contract must set quality standards, give the firm the right to inspect and audit sales records, fix a minimum royalty, and state how the licence can be ended if the terms are broken.
markingPoints: Calculates the yearly royalty of J$3,000,000 and J$9,000,000 over three years
Calculates own production as J$13,500,000 profit less J$15,000,000, a J$1,500,000 shortfall
Compares return and risk of both options
Identifies the risks of licensing, such as quality and honest reporting
Makes a justified recommendation with protective terms such as registration, quality checks and audit rights

essays.stem: A Montego Bay craft company finds that a website overseas is selling copies of its registered designs and using its brand name. Describe the steps you would take in response.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would collect evidence: screenshots of the website with dates, copies of the product listings and prices, and, if possible, a test purchase to show the goods are copies. I would check our own records to confirm what we own: the trade mark and design registrations, the countries they cover and their renewal dates. I would then seek advice from an attorney who deals with intellectual property, because the rules and the best route depend on the country involved. Depending on the advice, the first formal step would usually be a letter asking the seller to stop selling the copies and to remove our brand. Many online marketplaces and website hosts also have a procedure for owners to report goods that infringe their rights, and this can get listings removed quickly. If the seller ignores us and the losses are serious, the attorney could advise on legal action in the country concerned, weighing the cost against the likely benefit. Meanwhile, I would tell our customers clearly where to buy genuine products. Finally, I would review whether we need to register our rights in more countries and set up regular checks of online markets.
markingPoints: Collects dated evidence of the infringement
Checks the firm's own rights and where they apply
Seeks advice from an intellectual property attorney
Uses suitable steps: a letter to stop, platform reporting, and legal action if justified
Informs customers and strengthens protection and monitoring for the future

essays.stem: Evaluate franchising as a way for a successful Jamaican restaurant brand to use its intangible assets to grow.
essays.modelAnswer: Franchising lets the restaurant use its brand, recipes and way of operating to grow without paying for every new outlet itself. Franchisees invest their own money in premises and equipment and pay an initial fee and ongoing royalties, so the brand can expand faster and with less capital and risk than opening company-owned outlets. Local franchisees often know their towns well and, as owners, are usually more motivated than salaried managers. However, franchising has real drawbacks. The brand's reputation depends on many independent owners, and one poorly run outlet can harm the whole chain. The franchisor must invest in a detailed operations manual, training, supply arrangements and regular inspections to keep standards consistent. Profit per outlet is lower than for company-owned outlets, because most of the profit goes to the franchisee. Disputes over fees, territory and standards can arise, so the franchise agreement must be carefully drafted by an attorney. The brand and recipes must be properly protected first, with registered trade marks and confidentiality agreements. On balance, franchising is a strong option if the brand is well protected, the business model is proven and easy to copy, and the firm is ready to support and control its franchisees.
markingPoints: Explains how franchising uses the brand and systems to grow
Evaluates advantages: less capital, faster growth, motivated owners
Evaluates disadvantages: reputation risk, cost of support, lower profit per outlet, disputes
Identifies the need for protection and a well-drafted agreement
Reaches a balanced, justified conclusion

essays.stem: Explain how a firm should protect its digital intangible assets: its website and domain names, social media accounts, software and databases.
essays.modelAnswer: The firm should register its domain names in the firm's own name, not that of a staff member or web designer, and set them to renew automatically with reminders to a named manager. It may also register similar names and common misspellings to stop others using them. Social media accounts should be opened in the firm's name, with passwords held securely by the firm, two-step login turned on and at least two authorised administrators, so that the firm does not lose control when a person leaves. Software it buys must be properly licensed, with a record of licences, while software it has written for it should be covered by contracts that give the firm ownership of the code. Source code should be backed up and access limited. Customer and business databases should be stored on secure systems with access controls, passwords and encryption where possible, and backed up regularly to a separate location. Because databases often hold personal data, the firm must also follow the data protection law. Staff should be trained in good security habits, such as spotting phishing emails. Finally, the firm should list these assets in its register and review their security every year.
markingPoints: Registers and renews domain names in the firm's own name
Controls social media accounts with secure, shared administration
Manages software licences and ownership of commissioned code
Secures and backs up databases and follows the data protection law
Trains staff, records the assets and reviews security regularly

essays.stem: Much of a family firm's value lies in the know-how of a few long-serving staff. Recommend how the firm should protect and make use of this knowledge, and justify your recommendations.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first identify the critical know-how: which processes, customer relationships and technical skills depend on one or two people, and what would happen if they left. I would then recommend capturing it. The experts should be asked, and given time, to write down key procedures, with photographs or short videos, and these records should be stored securely as company documents. This is justified because written procedures stay with the firm and can be used to train others. Next, I would pair each expert with one or two staff members who learn the work by doing it alongside them, through job shadowing and mentoring. This spreads knowledge so that the firm does not depend on one person. I would make sure employment contracts include confidentiality terms and that the records are treated as confidential, so that the know-how does not pass to rivals. To keep the experts, I would recognise and reward their contribution, for example by naming them as trainers or giving them a role in improving processes, since they are more likely to share knowledge when they feel valued. Finally, the firm can use the documented know-how to train new staff faster, improve quality and, in time, license or franchise its methods.
markingPoints: Identifies which know-how is critical and the risk of losing it
Recommends documenting procedures and storing them securely
Recommends spreading knowledge through shadowing and mentoring
Protects know-how through confidentiality and keeps experts motivated
Justifies each recommendation and shows how the knowledge can be used

essays.stem: Explain why a business might need to value its intangible assets, and evaluate the difficulties of doing so.
essays.modelAnswer: A business may need to value its intangible assets when it is being sold or is buying another business, because much of the price may be for the brand, customer relationships and know-how rather than buildings and equipment. A value is also needed when licensing or franchising, to set fair royalties, when seeking finance, since some lenders and investors will consider strong brands and patents, when bringing in a new partner, when settling a dispute or claim for infringement, and when deciding how much to spend on protecting each asset. Valuing them is difficult for several reasons. Intangible assets are not traded in an open market like vehicles, so there is often no price to compare with. Their value depends on future income, which must be forecast and is uncertain. Many intangibles, such as reputation or staff know-how, work together and cannot easily be separated. Values can change quickly, for example after a scandal or a new rival product. For these reasons, accounting rules usually do not allow a firm to show a brand it built itself on its balance sheet. Firms often use specialist valuers and more than one method, and should treat any valuation as an estimate.
markingPoints: Explains valuation for sale or purchase of a business
Explains valuation for licensing, finance, partnership or disputes
Identifies the lack of a market price and reliance on uncertain forecasts
Identifies difficulties of separating assets and rapid changes in value
Notes accounting treatment or the use of specialist valuers and treating values as estimates

essays.stem: A firm's reputation is one of its most valuable intangible assets. Describe how a manager should protect and make use of the reputation of a hotel in Ocho Rios.
essays.modelAnswer: To protect the reputation, the manager should first make sure the service itself is reliably good, because reputation follows experience. That means clear standards for cleanliness, safety and guest service, staff trained to meet them, and regular checks. The hotel should monitor what guests say, through comment cards, online review sites and social media, and respond to complaints quickly, politely and in public where a review is public, showing what has been done to fix the problem. A simple crisis plan should set out who speaks for the hotel and what is said if something serious happens, such as a guest injury or a health problem, so that the response is fast, honest and consistent. Staff should understand that what they post online can affect the hotel. The brand name and logo should be registered as trade marks. To make use of the reputation, the manager can feature genuine guest reviews and awards in marketing, use the hotel's good name to win corporate and wedding business, negotiate better terms with tour operators, and attract good staff. A strong reputation can also support higher room rates and, in time, partnerships or new branches that carry the same name.
markingPoints: Protects reputation through consistent service standards and training
Monitors feedback and reviews and responds to complaints properly
Has a crisis communication plan and guidance for staff online
Protects the name legally through trade mark registration
Uses the reputation actively in marketing, sales, pricing and partnerships

practical1.title: Audit a firm's intangible assets and plan their protection
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up business (for example a Kingston food company with a popular sauce brand, a website, a customer database and two long-serving cooks, or a Negril tour company with a well-known name, social media accounts and agent contracts). The pack includes staff interview notes, sample contracts and a list of registrations, with some gaps and risks hidden in it. As a group, carry out an audit of the firm's intangible assets and produce: an intangible asset register in a spreadsheet (at least ten assets, each with its type, owner, current protection, renewal date where it applies, importance and risk); a list of the gaps and risks found; and a one-page protection action plan with priorities, owners, costs and dates. Give each member a named role: audit lead (keeps time and assembles the pack), brand and digital assets officer, contracts and people officer (checks the employment and contractor terms), register keeper (builds the spreadsheet), and action planner (writes the action plan). In a group of four, the audit lead also writes the action plan. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
photos: The flipchart brainstorm of the firm's intangible assets, grouped by type
The intangible asset register on screen
The list of gaps and risks found in the case pack
The contract review notes showing missing confidentiality or ownership terms
The finished protection action plan with priorities, owners and dates
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Identified a wide range of intangible assets, not only registered rights
Matched each asset to a suitable form of protection
Found the gaps and risks hidden in the case pack
Action plan sets realistic priorities based on value and risk
Kept the case information confidential and the register secure
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up case and do not copy real firms' logos or names
Keep the register and contracts confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Prepare and negotiate a brand licensing proposal
practical2.brief: Your group works for a made-up Jamaican firm that owns a registered brand (for example a juice or a skin-care brand). A manufacturer overseas, played by the assessor or a volunteer, wants a licence to make and sell products under the brand. First, prepare a licensing proposal of two pages: the reasons to license, the risks and how they will be managed, and the heads of terms (territory, products, duration, royalty rate and minimum payment, quality standards and inspection, reporting and audit, use of the brand, and how the licence ends). Include royalty forecasts for three years at two possible sales levels, worked and checked twice. Next, hold a 20-minute negotiation meeting with the licensee, run as a role play, and record the agreed points and any open issues. Finally, write a one-page summary for the firm's board. Give each member a named role: lead negotiator (opens and leads the meeting), finance officer (royalty forecasts), terms writer (heads of terms), risk officer (risks and quality controls), and note-taker (records the meeting and writes the board summary). In a group of four, the lead negotiator also writes the board summary. Photograph each stage and hand in the proposal, the meeting notes and the summary.
materials: Brief on the brand and the licensee from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
photos: The flipchart showing the group's aims and limits for the negotiation
The royalty forecasts on screen at both sales levels, with the second check marked
The negotiation meeting in progress (notes and table only if anyone prefers no face)
The record of agreed points and open issues
The one-page summary for the board
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Royalty forecasts are correct and were checked twice
Heads of terms protect the brand: quality, inspection, reporting and ending the licence
Risks are identified with practical controls
Negotiated politely and firmly, keeping to the group's agreed limits
Board summary accurately records what was agreed and what is still open
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Treat the negotiation brief and figures as confidential
Use only the made-up brand and do not copy real brands or logos
Stay respectful in the negotiation and disagree with positions, not people
Ask permission before photographing anyone and share the speaking fairly
